channel.title: Responsible AI & Neurodivergence, Naba Rizvi
channel.description: Daily curated research feed on ethical and responsible AI, with emphasis on neurodivergent people and serious mental illness.

item.title: AI Psychosis in Context: How Conversation History Shapes LLM Responses to Delusional Beliefs
item.description: Five frontier models were handed the same escalating delusional conversation history at three levels of accumulated context, with every response coded on risk and safety by two human raters plus qualitative analysis. The models split cleanly into two tiers, and crucially added context pushed them further apart, degrading the unsafe group while activating stronger safety behaviour in the safer one. The failure modes were validating a user's delusional premise, elaborating new content beyond it, and attempting harm reduction from inside the delusional frame, whereas safer models used the established relationship as leverage to challenge the belief and direct the person outward. The practical implication is that short context evaluations mischaracterise safety in both directions, and that delusion reinforcement looks like a tractable alignment problem rather than an inevitability.

item.title: LLM Psychosis: A Theoretical and Diagnostic Framework for Reality-Boundary Failures in Large Language Models
item.description: This paper argues that hallucination is the wrong word for a family of failures in which a model loses the boundary between the world and whatever premise it has been handed, and proposes five hallmarks: reality boundary dissolution, persistence of injected false beliefs, incoherence under impossible constraints, self model instability, and epistemic overconfidence. It operationalises them as a five axis Cognitive Integrity Scale and reports an adversarial probe battery against a current frontier model, sorting results into a three tier severity taxonomy. The most consequential claim for deployed systems is the delusional gradient, where correction pressure deepens rather than resolves the failure. Worth reading alongside the clinical work with some care, since borrowing psychiatric vocabulary for machine behaviour can carry stigma back the other way.

item.title: Ethical Evaluation of AI-Supported Mental Health Applications
item.description: The study combines a literature review, a structured assessment of four widely used mental health applications across fourteen categories, and grounded theory interviews with practising psychiatrists. The application audit found gaps in transparency, accountability, crisis detection and clinical accuracy, while the interviews surfaced four themes: an ontological mismatch with psychiatry, clinical role displacement, the limits of digital empathy, and clinicians' own emotional reactions to these tools. Read against psychiatric ethics norms and the four biomedical principles, the conclusion is that no ethical framework yet exists that is built specifically for psychiatric AI rather than borrowed wholesale from general medical ethics.

item.title: Beyond Labels: Realism and Participatory Design as Keys to Effective AI-Based Neurodiversity Training in the Workplace
item.description: Grounded in the double empathy problem, this study tested whether brief AI generated gamified scenarios, using either diagnostic disclosure or plain behavioural description, could shift how 86 participants judged autistic peers and how willing they were to engage with them. The finding that matters for design is that realism carried the intervention, and low fidelity synthetic scenarios landed in the uncanny valley and undercut the message they were meant to deliver. The authors conclude that workplace inclusion training has to move past information sharing toward co-created, emotionally authentic material, and that the burden of communicative adaptation belongs with neurotypical colleagues rather than with autistic employees.

item.title: Irresponsible Counselors: Large Language Models and the Loneliness of Modern Humans
item.description: The argument here is structural rather than empirical: general purpose models have slid into the role of always available, inexpensive, seemingly nonjudgmental counsellors on health, relationships, money and identity, while remaining stateless systems with no subjectivity, intention or answerability. The authors name the result advisory intimacy without a subject, a relation in which outputs are received as understanding and neutrality even though no agent stands behind them. They contend that the familiar framings of developer liability, dataset bias and parasocial attachment do not reach the actual configuration, and trace the consequences for policy, for justice in who can access real counselling, and for how loneliness itself is understood.

item.title: AI Act: Transparency Rules and Enforcement Powers Take Effect
item.description: As of 2 August 2026 the AI Act is applicable, the AI Office and national authorities hold enforcement powers, and the transparency rules are live. For mental health and companion products the operative duty is that people must be told they are talking to a machine and that generated content be identifiable. The high risk obligations that would bite hardest on employment screening, education and access to essential services were pushed back to December 2027 by the AI Omnibus that entered into force in July, so the fairness relevant duties around data quality, human oversight and discrimination risk are still ahead rather than in effect. A separate prohibition on non consensual sexual and abusive generated imagery begins in December 2026.
